newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- JAN 21.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- JAN 21.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek general press:

--The government has been transformed into a passive bystander, unable to effectively intervene to contain the enormous economic and social cost of the wave of strikes hitting the country. Seamen last night decided to extend their strike for another 48 hours, worsening problems for farmers on Crete while teachers yesterday joined in with their five-day rolling strikes.

--There has been a difference of views noted in relations between Athens and Nicosia over Cyprus accession to the European Union. Sources say last Friday's meeting in Athens saw Cyprus President Glafcos Clerides insisting that if the matter of EU accession was not included in talks to resolve the Cyprus issue then the negotiations would be still-born. Athens opposes.

--Reports yesterday said that the widow of late prime minister Andreas Papandreou, Dimitra Liani, was thinking of selling the notorious "pink villa" in the plush outer suburb of Ekali. Although denied by Liani's associates last night, Liani is thought to be unable to keep up the cost of the villa - estimated at 1.5 million drachmas a month - on her monthly pension of 345,000 drachmas. If put on the market, the property is expected to fetch 800 million - one billion drachmas.

--There was tension at the port of Piraeus early yesterday as truck drivers and dockworkers traded blows. A Supreme Court prosecutor has given the go-ahead for prosecution of those found to be obstructing loading and unloading of vessels. Teachers, meanwhile, greeted their five-day strike with an 80 percent participation rate while the government pleaded with them for dialogue.

--Government spokesman Dimitris Reppas yesterday was critical about Education Minister Gerasimos Arsenis's reservations over initiatives by outsiders in Greece's national issues as Prime Minister Costas Simitis flew to Rome for a meeting of the Socialist International.

--Alarming noises from Ankara as Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash condemns the Cypriot missile purchase and threatens "diplomatic union" with Ankara and an infusion of mainland settlers into the ghost-town of Varosha in occupied Cyprus.

--The first major opinion poll of the year sees ruling party PASOK and Prime Minister Costas Simitis galloping ahead of main opposition New Democracy and its leader Miltiades Evert. Simitis is second most popular leader (54.2 percent), after Coalition of the Left and Progress leader Nikos Constantopoulos (63.5 percent). Evert brings up the rear with 20.8 percent.
--Mistakes on car registration notices have caused chaos in payment.
--Nude scenes from new Greek film "The Bachelor" will be cut following the settlement of differences between director Nikos Panayiotopoulos and actor Leda Matsangou.
--Subsidies for holidays for low-income earners and pensioners under the "social tourism" programme have been reduced substantially. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
